title: Azure.Identity
description: Authenticate with Azure services using managed identities, service principals, and developer credentials.

data.text: `Azure.Identity` provides credential classes for authenticating Azure SDK clients. It supports `DefaultAzureCredential`, `ManagedIdentityCredential`, and developer-friendly credentials like `VisualStudioCredential`.
`DefaultAzureCredential` tries multiple credential sources in order, making it easy to write code that works locally and in Azure.

data.title: Authenticate with DefaultAzureCredential

terms.definition: A chained credential that tries multiple authentication methods automatically.
An identity managed by Azure for cloud resources, eliminating the need for secrets.
The base interface used by all Azure SDK identity credentials.

data.title: Best Practice
data.text: Use `DefaultAzureCredential` for most scenarios. It works in Azure and on your local machine without code changes.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: `DefaultAzureCredential` is the recommended choice for most apps.
No need to manage connection strings when using managed identities.
All modern Azure SDK clients accept `TokenCredential`.
data.takeaway: Azure.Identity simplifies authentication across all Azure services with a single, consistent API.

data.title: Exercise: Authenticate with DefaultAzureCredential
data.description: Replace a hardcoded connection string with DefaultAzureCredential in a small console app.
steps: Install Azure.Identity and an Azure SDK package.
Replace the connection string with `new DefaultAzureCredential()`.
Run locally with Azure CLI logged in.
data.expectedOutcome: You understand how DefaultAzureCredential works and can use it with any Azure SDK client.
